children: If that **activation goes up**, its contribution to done goes up, because the contribution is the activation times a positive weight. So the **probability of done goes up**.
If that **weight goes up**, from 0.1 to 0.2, the same contribution gets bigger, because the activation is positive. So the **probability of done goes up** again.
**A positive number times a positive number is positive.** So raising either one makes that neuron push the done output up more.

teaching.text: These questions test whether you understand what happens, not whether you can multiply. A good answer names the direction, up or down, and then gives the reason. For example, "the probability of done goes up because the weight and the activation are both positive, so their product adds more to the done output."
children: In plain terms, each neuron votes for each output through its weight. A positive vote from an active neuron always helps that output.
If the weight were negative instead, raising the activation would push the output down. So the sign of the weight decides the direction.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Every network starts out knowing nothing**, because its weights start out **random**. It only gets better when it is told the right answer.
children: The right answer is given as a **desired output**. For a recording of dean, the desired output is **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**. This says there is a 100 percent chance it was dean and zero chance for every other word. A list like this, with one 1 and zeros everywhere else, is called a **one-hot encoding**.
The output the network actually produces is the **computed output**. The difference between the computed output and the desired output is the network's **error**.
The desired outputs come from real data, such as a table of each student's formants together with the vowel that student actually said.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the method that changes the weights so the network makes better decisions. After learning, if you give the network 320 and 2000 again, the probability of done should go down and the probability of dean should go up.
children: **Learning happens gradually, one small step at a time.** Just like stochastic gradient descent, the weights do not jump to the right values all at once. Each piece of data nudges the weights a little, then the next piece nudges them again, and so on.
Each weight moves a small step in whichever direction makes the error smaller. The **learning rate** sets how big each step is.

The weights are updated **starting from the end**. First the weights into the output change, then the weights into the third hidden layer, then the second, then the first. During this backward pass, the activations from the forward pass stay the same.

teaching.text: This is why AI needs huge **data centers**. A modern chatbot can have **trillions of weights**, and backpropagation has to nudge every one of them, over and over, for months.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the **last weight**, it is easy to tell which way to change it. This is the 0.1 that connects the top neuron of the last hidden layer to **done**.
children: That weight multiplies an activation of about 1.57, so raising the weight would raise the probability of done.
The desired probability of done is **zero**, so raising the weight would make the error **worse**.
So that weight should be **lowered**. Lowering it shrinks its contribution and pulls the probability of done down toward zero. Only one inner product is needed to figure this out.

teaching.text: For the **first weight**, it is very hard to tell which way to change it. This is the 0.005 near the input.
children: Changing it changes one activation in the first hidden layer. That changes the second hidden layer, which changes the third, which finally changes the output probabilities.

**Its effect on the decision has to pass through all the layers in between**, and it also depends on all the later weights. So you cannot tell just by looking at it whether it should go up or down. Backpropagation still works it out.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **The last weights directly control the output probabilities.** So they have a direct effect on the error, and the difference between the computed output and the desired output can be used right away to improve them.

**The first weights affect their own activations, and those activations then affect two more layers.** It is very hard to figure out how much an early weight is to blame for a mistake at the very end. Its effect on the error also **includes the effect of the last weights**, because the last weights come after it.

So **improving the last weights is the easy problem**, and improving the first weights is a much bigger problem that already contains the easy one. **Dynamic programming** is a method that solves the small problems first and then uses their answers to solve the bigger problems that depend on them. It was developed by **Bellman** and **Viterbi**.
children: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.** Stochastic gradient descent changes the numbers gradually. Dynamic programming decides the order, which is the **back** in backpropagation.
Backpropagation was worked out in the **mid-1980s**. In 2024, a Nobel Prize recognized it, because there would be no AI without it.

Research from the last ten years suggests that single neurons in the brain also work forward and then backward, using their chemistry. So this forward-then-backward process may not be so different from what brains do.

The short exam answer is this. The last weight affects the decision in one simple step. The first weight's effect passes through many layers and depends on the later weights. So the easy problem is solved first, and its answer is reused for the harder problems.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training needs two tables of numbers, which are called **matrices**. Each row pairs **one recording** with **the vowel it really was**.
children: The **input matrix** has one row per recording and **two columns**, F1 and F2, because the network takes in two numbers. With about 110 recordings, it is 110 by 2.
The **output matrix** has one row per recording and **five columns**, one for each word. A **1 marks the true vowel**, and the other columns have 0. It is 110 by 5.
So row by row, the network is told the right answer. For example, formants like 800 and 1700 go with one vowel, and formants like 700 and 1100 go with another.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python** program that uses the **PyTorch** library builds and trains this network.
children: The **import** lines tell the program to use the **torch library**. The library does all the background work, so the network can be described in just a few lines.
The two **load** lines read in the two matrices. The formants become X, and the true vowels become Y.

teaching.text: **Sequential** means the network is a **sequence of layers**, one after another. **Linear** means the layer **does inner products**, because a linear layer only multiplies and adds.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** describes the **first hidden layer**, which takes **2 inputs and gives 3 outputs**. The next lines take 3 and give 2, take 2 and give 4, and take 4 and give 5.

The network has **five layers**, but there are only **four lines**, because the **input layer does no processing**. It only receives numbers, so the only sign of it in the code is the 2 in the first line.

teaching.text: The last lines run **one training step** using all 110 rows at once. **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, and **lr** is the **learning rate**, which sets the size of each step.
children: The **loss** measures the network's mistakes by comparing its outputs with the true vowels. **backward** runs backpropagation to work out how each weight should change, and **step** actually changes the weights.
In plain terms, the program describes the network, shows it the data, measures how wrong it is, works backward to find which weights caused the mistake, and then adjusts the weights a little.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932** for discovering that **neurons are nearly digital**. A real neuron is roughly **on or off**. It is either firing or not firing, instead of taking any value at all. The neurons in the network so far are not like that, because their activations can be any number, such as slightly below zero, about 6.6, or about 2.7.
Because of this discovery, people added an **activation function** called the **sigmoid** to neural networks. The sigmoid takes the inner product and squashes it into a number between zero and one.
children: If the inner product is a **large negative number**, the sigmoid gives about **0**, so the neuron is **off**. An inner product of minus 4 gives almost exactly zero, and minus 10, minus 100 and minus 1000 also give about zero.
If the inner product is a **large positive number**, the sigmoid gives about **1**, so the neuron is **on**. An inner product of 4 gives almost exactly one, and 6 or 100 also give about one.

Only inner products **near zero** give values in between. So the sigmoid makes the neuron **nearly digital**, either on or off. This is like the chemistry that keeps real neurons from firing without limit.

teaching.text: The sigmoid also matches something important about **perception** in animals and humans. **Some things that are very different are perceived as the same, and some things that are very similar are perceived as different.**
children: You recognize a friend as the same person whether they wear a hat or not, or a different shirt on a different day. Perception ignores many real differences, just as the sigmoid gives minus 1000, minus 100 and minus 20 all the same value.

USC and UCLA are close to each other, both large, and alike in their labs and their football. Yet people see them as completely different. Small differences can matter a lot, just as two inputs slightly below and slightly above zero land on opposite sides of the sigmoid's jump.
In plain terms, the flat parts of the curve treat very different inputs as the same, and the steep middle separates inputs that are almost the same.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Adding the sigmoid to each hidden neuron changes every number that comes after it. The inputs are still the formants, but each hidden neuron now passes on its sigmoid value instead of its raw inner product.
children: The first hidden neuron's inner product is slightly below zero, and the sigmoid turns it into about **0.4**.
The second neuron's inner product is about 6.6, and the sigmoid turns it into about **1**, so that neuron is fully on.
Each time a neuron changes, the activations in the later layers are recalculated, and the output probabilities shift.

teaching.text: With the same random weights and the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons, the decision moves away from done. The network now spreads its probability more evenly and gives its highest probability, about one third, to **Dan**. So it is **still wrong** about dean.
children: The sigmoid changes how the network calculates, but only training with backpropagation can give it good weights.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program changes in only one way. **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each **hidden** linear layer. It means "apply the sigmoid," and it makes that layer nearly digital.
children: The **last layer has no sigmoid**, because its outputs go straight into the loss calculation, which turns them into probabilities with softmax.
The rest of the training program, with SGD and a learning rate of 0.1, stays the same.

teaching.text: To find out whether the sigmoid makes the vowel recognizer better or worse, you train both versions and compare them. You can also swap in other activation functions that look somewhat like the sigmoid, such as one called **ReLU**, to see whether they improve recognition.
children: **Many of the most basic ideas in AI come from how real brains work.** These include neurons, inner products that collect input from many neurons, and the nearly digital firing that the sigmoid copies.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** copies a very simple piece of human perception. It takes the **two formants**, F1 and F2, of a single vowel said on its own, and it decides which of five words it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**. It has 2 input neurons, hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 output neurons. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

**The weights are the network's knowledge.** Each weight is a positive or negative number. For each recording, the network is told the right answer as a probability distribution. For a speaker's /i/, it is told **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**, which means a 100 percent chance that the word was dean.
children: At first, **the weights are random**, so the network knows nothing. The distribution it produces is usually very different from the right answer.
That difference is a **mistake**, and the network learns by correcting its mistakes.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network. Take **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, which is one speaker's /i/. Each neuron in the first hidden layer computes an **inner product**, which means it multiplies each formant by its weight and adds the results. Those activations go into the next layer, which does its own inner products. This continues until the output gives a probability for each word.
children: With random weights, the network gives its highest probability, more than half, to **done**. So it decides it heard done, even though the right answer is dean.

teaching.text: To fix the mistake, **all the weights have to change**, both the ones near the output and the ones near the input. The method that does this is **backpropagation**, which combines **stochastic gradient descent** and **dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: **Changing a weight at the very end changes the output probabilities right away.** The output probabilities are the network's decision, and the last weights are exactly the ones used in the final inner products.
children: For example, the probability of done comes partly from a weight of 0.1 times an activation of about 1.57.

The network said done, but the answer was dean, so the probability of done is **too high**. Raising that 0.1 to 0.5 would make the probability of done even higher, which is the opposite of what we want. So that weight should go **down**.
For the last weights, it is easy to tell whether each one should go up or down.

teaching.text: **Changing a weight near the input sets off a chain of changes.** It changes the activations in the first hidden layer. Those change the second hidden layer, which changes the third, which finally changes the decision.
children: So deciding how to change an early weight is a very hard problem. It is like the dynamic programming puzzle where always picking the smallest next step gives the wrong answer.

sections.title: Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The real formant data from the class shows why AI is hard. Each recording is a dot. **F1 is on the horizontal axis**, and **F2 is on the vertical axis**. There are 525 dots, 105 for each vowel.
children: The data does show a pattern. The **/i/ dots are high up**, with a **high F2 and a low F1**, just as the theory predicts. And /i/ is clearly different from /u/.
But there is **a huge amount of overlap**. Many /æ/ dots sit among the /i/ dots, and many others overlap with schwa. The /u/, /a/ and schwa groups of dots pile on top of each other.
Some dots are probably measurement mistakes. Real data always has errors, the same way speech recorded by a phone on a noisy train has errors. So these dots were left in.

teaching.text: **If each vowel's dots formed its own separate group, AI would be easy.** Because the groups overlap, a network has to see the data many times to learn where each vowel is most likely. Even then, many points are unclear. If a new speaker's formants land in the middle of the overlap, the best the network can do is pick the vowel whose dots are most common there.
children: People tried for about seventy years to remove the differences between speakers, which is called **normalization**, without success. Hearing a lot of speech from the same speaker does help, because it gives the system more information about that person.

This overlap was first discovered in the early 1950s by **Peterson and Barney**. During the Second World War, spectrograms were kept secret by the military, and the overlap was found once spectrograms became available.

Good speech recognition only arrived around 2011 or 2012, using neural networks trained by backpropagation. Surprisingly, speech that changes over time turned out to be easier for modern systems than this frozen, one-moment problem.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** is the same method used to improve an average from data. Here it is used to improve every weight. It has the same **learning rate**, with the same tradeoff between learning fast and learning accurately.

**Dynamic programming** decides the order. The weights at the end are improved first, then the weights before them, and so on back to the beginning. So the easiest problem is solved first, and the hardest problem is solved last.
children: The error tells the network which way each output should move. Done, at about 56 percent, should go down. Dean should go up, and the other words should go down.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the last weights, one inner product connects each weight to the decision, so the direction of the change is clear. The network said done when the answer was dean. So any last weight that pushes done up should be **lowered**, and any last weight that pushes dean up should be **raised**.
children: A good exam answer says which way the weight should move and then explains why. Name the activation the weight multiplies and the output it feeds into.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Backpropagation changes the last weights first, then the weights before them, and so on back to the first weights.** Each problem gets easier because something has already been learned from the problems solved before it.
children: Modern systems use this same method on about **six trillion weights**. That is what the huge data centers are doing.
**Geoffrey Hinton** won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for backpropagation. This idea is at the center of much of today's economy, and it has roots in physics through dynamical systems.
In plain terms, it is easiest to blame the weights closest to the mistake. That blame is then passed backward to the weights that came before them.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training uses **two matrices** of numbers. The first has one row per recording with **F1 and F2**. The second has a matching row of **zeros and a single one**, which marks the vowel the recording really was. During learning, the network picks a row, makes its decision, and compares it with the true answer. If the decision is wrong, the weights change.

**If the network makes the right decision, there is no error, so it has nothing to learn.** This can be a real problem. A network can keep getting the right answer by **memorizing** its data without learning the real pattern underneath. Stopping the learning at that point would be stopping too early.
Children learning English show the same thing, as **Carol Chomsky** observed in the early 1960s.
children: At first, very young children say **go** and **went** correctly, because they are just **memorizing** what they hear.
Then they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs make the past tense by adding a sound at the end, as in **jump** and **jumped**. So they start saying **goed**.
Later, they learn that some verbs are **exceptions**, and they get both the regular verbs and the exceptions right.
In plain terms, a right answer early on can come from memory, and real learning can show up as new mistakes.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: **The import lines bring into Python the programs for inner products, backpropagation and related work**, so none of that has to be written by hand. The exam can ask what these lines mean, but it will never ask you to write the program from scratch.
children: This works because of **libraries**. A library is a collection of programs written by one group that other people can use without knowing how they work inside. The idea of building software this way goes back to **Margaret Hamilton's** work on the software that flew **Apollo 11** to the moon.

Around 2015, **Facebook** released **PyTorch** and **Google** released **TensorFlow**. After that, researchers no longer had to write their own backpropagation code. Most people now use PyTorch, which is often just called torch.
The **load** lines read the formant matrix and the matching vowel matrix from files on the computer.

teaching.text: **Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers**, one after another. Every network covered so far is like this. A large language model is an example of a network that is not just a sequence of layers.
children: Each **Linear** line is one **processing layer**. A processing layer has weights and does inner products with the numbers coming in. The input layer does no processing, so the five layers need only **four lines**.
**nn.Linear(2, 3)** means "this layer receives information from 2 neurons, and it has 3 neurons." The other lines read the same way.

teaching.text: The last lines are all PyTorch needs for learning.
children: **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, and **lr** is the **learning rate**, set here to 0.1. **A higher learning rate learns much faster but less accurately. A lower learning rate learns more accurately but much more slowly.**
So changing the learning rate from 0.1 to 0.3 makes the network **learn faster**, but its **accuracy goes down**.
**Loss** is the measure of the **mistake**. The program calculates the mistakes so it can learn from them. **backward** runs **backpropagation**, and **step** updates the weights.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: Artificial neural networks borrow their basic ideas from discoveries about real brains. Real brains have **neurons**, and each neuron **collects information from many other neurons**, which is what the inner product does.

**Lord Edgar Adrian** discovered in the 1920s that **neurons are nearly digital**, and he won the **Nobel Prize in 1932**. A real neuron is either **firing** or **not firing**. It is not at some level in between like 2, 16 or 34. But the neurons in the network so far have activations that can be any number, like slightly below zero, 6.64, 2.72 and 1.57.
The **sigmoid** is an **activation function** that makes the network work more like Adrian's discovery. It takes an inner product and gives back a number between zero and one.
children: An inner product of **minus 4**, minus 6 or minus 1000 gives about **zero**, so the neuron is **off**.
An inner product of **2** gives about 0.8 or 0.9. An inner product of **4**, 6 or 100 gives about **one**, so the neuron is **on**.
So the sigmoid makes neural processing **nearly digital**, the way brain chemistry does. Without that limit, an activation of a thousand would be like lightning coming out of someone's head.

teaching.text: The sigmoid also matches perception. **Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.** Very different large negative inputs all come out as off. But two nearly equal inputs on either side of the steep middle come out as one off and one on.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Adding the sigmoid one hidden neuron at a time changes the whole calculation after it. Each neuron's raw inner product is replaced by its sigmoid value. Then every later activation is recalculated, and the output probabilities shift.
children: The first hidden neuron, slightly below zero, becomes about 0.4. The second, about 6.6, becomes nearly 1.
With the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons and the same random weights, the network's choice moves from done to Dan. So it is still wrong until it is trained.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: In the program, **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each hidden linear layer. It means "apply the sigmoid," and it makes that layer nearly digital. The last layer gets no sigmoid, because its outputs go into the loss calculation.
children: The sigmoid can also be replaced by other functions that look somewhat like it, such as **ReLU**. Trying them out shows whether they make recognition better or worse.
**AI copies abilities that animals have.** Its most basic ideas come from biologists' discoveries about how brains work. Computer scientists then add their own ideas on top.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: The full training program runs **2000 updates**. Each update uses all the recordings, with a learning rate of 0.1. The formants are first divided by a thousand, which turns hertz into kilohertz. After every update, the program records the **accuracy**, which is the percent of recordings the network gets right. The word with the highest score counts as the network's answer.

**The accuracy starts at 20 percent.** With random weights, the network knows nothing. But with **five vowels**, even a random guess is right **one time out of five**, which is 20 percent. That level is called **chance**.
children: With **ten categories**, chance would be **10 percent**, because a random guess would be right one time in ten.

teaching.text: After a while, the accuracy **jumps up to about 40 percent**, which shows the network is learning something. Then it **levels off**, ending near **45 percent**. Each pass of learning is called an **epoch**, and a problem like this takes thousands of epochs.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: Training was repeated **ten times** on the same data. Each run started from a **different set of random weights**. A starting set of random numbers is called a **seed**, but the word itself will not be on the exam.
children: The runs take **different paths**. One run stays at chance for about 500 epochs before jumping up. Another jumps up very early, and another climbs more slowly.
**All ten runs end at the same accuracy**, close to 45 percent. Learning by stochastic gradient descent always involves chance along the way, but the end point is the same.

teaching.text: Children learning language are similar. One child's family might talk mostly about sports, and another child's family might talk mostly about politics. So each child hears very different words and voices. But by about age four, both children speak the same language, because the basic patterns under their different experiences are the same.

**The network levels off near 40 percent, not 100 percent, because the vowel data overlap so much.** For a point in the middle of the overlap, even a person looking carefully at the data would have to guess. AI is not magic, so a problem that is very hard for people is also hard for machines.
children: The next experiment is to add or remove layers, or change the number of neurons in each layer, to see whether the 40 percent gets better or worse.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes in information about one moment, uses its **weights** to process it, and makes a decision. It learns those weights by making mistakes and correcting them through **backpropagation**. The idea began in **1943** with a paper by **McCulloch and Pitts**, which proposed that simple math could model how the brain works.
children: The paper starts from the idea that nerve activity is **all-or-none**, where all means active and none means inactive. This is the same idea as the **sigmoid**. So the very first paper on artificial neural networks starts from biology, from how real neurons behave.
Warren McCulloch was a **psychiatrist**. The earliest work on neural networks tried to model how the mind works, including mental illness. It was not about making money.

teaching.text: By **1986**, these ideas had grown into the two **Parallel Distributed Processing** books, written by a group at UC San Diego. **Parallel** means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time. **Distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons.
children: By then, forward propagation and backpropagation were fully worked out. One of the contributors, **Geoffrey Hinton**, later won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for this work.

teaching.text: **Given one static vector of formants, these networks could choose between a few possible categories.** A **vector** is just a list of numbers, and static means one fixed list from one moment. But **human thinking is much more complex** than taking in one list of numbers and giving one decision at the end.
children: **Speech changes constantly over time**, because every tiny moment gives a new set of formants.
**Language changes over time too**, because a sentence is many words, one after another.
So a network that only gets one list of numbers can never model thinking that happens over time.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: In **1985**, **Michael Jordan** developed **recurrent neural networks** to understand **speech production**, which is how the tongue, the velum and the lips move over time. Features such as nasality, backness and lip rounding each turn on and off at different moments across a sequence of sounds. Jordan realized that a regular network could never handle something that complex and that changes so much over time.
children: His network is **not just sequential**, meaning it is not just one layer after another, because it has **two layers working side by side**.

It is called **recurrent** because it **takes its output and sends it back into part of its input**. It produces something at one moment, uses that to predict the next moment, and then uses that to predict the moment after.

teaching.text: **GPT works the same way, one word at a time.** It takes the words of the prompt and predicts the next word, which becomes the first word of its answer. Then it feeds the prompt plus that new word back in and predicts the next word again. It keeps going like this. So the idea behind GPT started in 1985, with thinking about how speech happens over time.
children: People kept improving the recurrent network from 1985 until **2017**, when the **large language model** was invented.

teaching.text: **Science and technology grow from other people's ideas over long periods of time.** An idea from 1943 was improved into the networks of 1986. Jordan's idea from 1985 was improved into the large language models of 2017. And the people who came up with these ideas were mostly not the people who made a lot of money from them.
children: These years help you understand the history, but they will not be on the exam.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: AI systems are built up in steps, and **each step is made from the one before it**.
children: **A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds them all up, which is the **inner product**. The symbol **sigma** just means add them up. This uses only second-grade multiplication and addition to model the electrical and chemical activity of a real neuron.

**A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a whole decision vector.** Its layers are connected by sets of weights. Each set of weights turns one vector into the next one through many inner products.

teaching.text: **A large language model takes in many vectors, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision vector about what comes next.** Picture 15 vectors, where each one stands for something at one moment, such as one word of a sentence. The model's job is to **predict the sixteenth**.
children: In real systems, there are hundreds of thousands to a million input vectors, and that set is called the **context window**. Each vector is also thousands of numbers long. That is why huge data centers are needed.
The sixteenth vector is a **probability distribution over the next word**. English has about 30,000 words, so each entry gives the chance that one particular word comes next.

teaching.text: **A large language model is made of neural networks.** Each set of weights is a **layer**, and real systems have about a hundred or more layers. **The knowledge is still in the weights.** So an LLM's knowledge of how to write an essay is stored in its weights.

**An LLM is a dynamical system**, and that is why the Nobel Prize for AI was given in physics. A mass-spring system starts from **initial conditions**, which are its starting position and speed, and its rules decide what happens next. An LLM's initial condition is its set of input vectors. Each layer turns them into **better vectors**, step after step, until the last layer can predict the next word.
children: The calculation at every step is the **inner product**, multiplying and adding billions or trillions of times.
In plain terms, an LLM is like the oscillator. But instead of two numbers changing over time, thousands of numbers are improved layer by layer.

teaching.text: **An LLM learns by predicting the next word and correcting its mistakes.** Take "the cat sat on the," where the real next word is **mat**. A new LLM with random weights might predict something impossible like "in." Backpropagation then adjusts its trillions of weights so its prediction moves toward mat.
children: After this is repeated with about a trillion sentences, the system surprisingly ends up knowing how to speak English.
The first problem this design solved, in 2017, was **machine translation**. The same design then worked for speech and many other problems.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a graph of LLMs**, which means several LLMs connected to each other. An **agent** in AI today is just an LLM.
children: An **outline LLM** receives the prompt and is told only to outline the answer. A **writing LLM** turns the outline into smooth sentences.

A **critic LLM** points out problems in the draft. A **revision LLM** decides whether the draft is good enough or sends it back to the critic, usually for only a few rounds. Then a **final LLM** produces the output.
The critic is what greatly reduced **hallucination**, which is when the system makes things up. The conversation between the LLMs inside the system is why many systems take a while to respond.

teaching.text: **Neurons make neural networks, neural networks make LLMs, and LLMs make agentic systems.** This is like how molecules make cells and cells make organs.
children: Designing a graph of LLMs to solve a problem is a real job today. It takes problem solving more than knowledge of programming languages.
The connections between LLMs can also form circuits that nobody planned. These circuits can let a system do things that were never part of the design, and sometimes those things are harmful.

teaching.text: **The main idea behind all of this is Gestalt completion.** People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though no triangle is drawn. A big part of human knowledge is **filling in** what is missing. Training a system only to **predict the missing piece** turns out to copy a big part of human thinking.
children: The same idea is behind the **cloze procedure**, a test introduced by **Wilson Taylor** in **1953**. In this test, words are removed from a text and people fill them in. The name comes from **closure**, the Gestalt term for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a broken circle as a whole circle.
**Knowledge can be tested by asking someone to complete a sequence, and for AI, completing sequences is all that knowledge is.** An LLM predicting the next word is playing a cloze game over and over.
Underneath everything, **inference is inner products**, and **learning is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: **An LLM takes 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth.** A vector is just a list of numbers, so those numbers can stand for almost anything. Whatever they stand for, the machine plays the same game of predicting the next one.

The vectors can be **words**. In "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," the sixteenth vector is the missing next word. A speaker of English knows a likely ending, such as branch or mat.
children: To get it right, the model has to use the whole sentence, because it was the cat, not the dog, that sat.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **slices of sound**. A spectrogram is cut into small frames, and each frame becomes one vector of frequencies and amplitudes. The system learns to predict the next small piece of speech from all the pieces before it.
children: In 2019, this approach gave the **best speech recognition in 75 years**. It is also the basis for synthetic voices that are now very hard to tell apart from real people.
The newest systems can hold a spoken conversation, and the only clue left is a slight delay before each response. As that delay gets shorter, phone scams become a real danger.

teaching.text: The vectors can be **pieces of an image**. An image is cut into **16 patches**, read row by row, and the system predicts the missing patch. After training on huge numbers of images, it learns what a dog, a dolphin or a boat is. This became the basis of modern **computer vision**.

The vectors can even be **amino acids**. A protein is a chain of amino acids, which come in **20 kinds**, and the order of the chain decides how the protein folds into its shape. Researchers treated a protein as just a sequence and played the same predict-the-next game. This pushed the **protein folding problem** many years ahead, which matters for designing drugs and vaccines.
children: That work won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry**.

teaching.text: **The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all reach it the same way. So the same design always asks the same question, which is what comes sixteenth.
children: These systems predict from past data. So when something new comes up that the past data does not cover, they can **hallucinate**.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English allows only **certain sequences of sounds** in its words. Knowing which sequences are allowed is part of every speaker's knowledge of the language. **A simple English syllable can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, mat, sit, cup, dog and fish.
children: The pattern is about **sounds, not letters**. The silent e in shave, kite and rope does not count. Two letters can also spell one consonant sound, as in ship, chin and bath.

teaching.text: Syllables can also have **clusters**, which are groups of consonants together. A cluster before the vowel is called an **onset**, as in split, flat and black. A cluster after the vowel is called a **coda**, as in desk, help and lamp. **Only certain sequences are allowed before the vowel and after the vowel.**
children: Each real word has an impossible twin marked with a star, such as **flat** and **lfat**, **help** and **hepl**, and **lamp** and **lapm**. Many twins use the same letters in a different order, so the order of the sounds matters.

**The order on one side of the vowel is the mirror image of the order on the other side.** In flat, the l is right next to the vowel and the f is farther out. In help, the l is again right next to the vowel, now on the other side, and the p is farther out. Each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables**, such as ba-na-na, At-lan-tic and ath-lete. The sounds t and l are fine when a syllable break falls between them. But **tl cannot start a syllable**, which is why Atlantic is a word but tlantic is impossible.
children: The sound **ng** can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one. So whether a sequence of sounds is allowed depends on where the syllable breaks fall.

teaching.text: **Every language has its own rules.** Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable. Cantonese also allows a final p. Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word. Spanish speakers turn a word like stadium into one that starts with e.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Knowing which sound sequences are allowed is called phonotactic knowledge, and it shows up in the same next-item game that GPT plays.** Each item is the beginning of an English word, and the task is to guess the next letter. People agree on their guesses quickly, and how much they agree changes from item to item.
**After a vowel, almost any letter can come next.** After "ra," likely letters include t, n, r and l, and many others are possible too.
**At the start of a word, the choices narrow sharply** to exactly what an English onset allows.
children: After **sp**, the next letter is l, r or a vowel, never n. After **k**, it is a vowel or n, as in knee, never t.
After **b** and **f**, it is r, l or a vowel, never n. After **sh**, it is a vowel or r, as in shrimp.
After **skr**, or after **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
After **bram**, the letter b is almost certain, as in bramble, though a new syllable could also start there.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item**, which is the same game an LLM plays. A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, because the only way its predictions can get good is by matching the patterns of English syllables.
children: Its prediction is a **probability distribution** over the next letter, and the shape of that distribution shows what it knows.
After "ra," the distribution is **flat**, spread over many letters. After "skr," it is **sharply peaked** on a few vowels, because English allows nothing else there.
In plain terms, the fewer letters English allows next, the more the probability piles onto those few letters.

sections.title: Build an LLM together

teaching.text: English syllables are a good test case for understanding LLMs. English has about 30,000 words, so training on words needs enormous amounts of data. But English has only about 26 letters, or a few dozen sounds. So a small LLM, with thousands of weights instead of trillions, can be trained to learn what every speaker already knows about English syllables.

Writing that program by hand would take months. So instead, the plan is to **design an agentic system using instructions written in English**. The agentic system builds the LLM, trains it to predict each next letter, and shows what it has learned along the way. Then its knowledge can be compared with what English speakers know about syllables.

lecture18.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: Everything in modern AI grows from **one very simple idea**. A **neuron** takes information from other neurons, multiplies each input by its weight, and adds them up. This is the **inner product**, and it stands in for the electrical and chemical signals that neurons send each other. People who move science forward usually start from very simple ideas like this one and then repeat them many times over.
children: A **neural network** repeats the inner product layer after layer. It takes a vector in and gives a **decision** out. Even something as complex as a person making a decision can be built from inner products and a function like the sigmoid, combined many times.
But a network that makes one **static decision**, such as hearing one vowel from two formants, cannot capture thinking that **happens over time**.

teaching.text: **Language depends on connections between words that are far apart.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, who live in a state far, far away," the next word is **barks**, not bark.
children: **Barks** goes with the singular word **dog**, no matter how many other words come in between, even plural words like parents.

No one teaches this rule directly. Speakers pick it up from the language around them. An LLM learns it the same way, from data. It uses its weights to do inner products, then more inner products, until it predicts barks.
English sentence structure, called **syntax**, is so complicated that many linguists spend their whole careers studying it. That is why an LLM needs so many layers of calculation.

teaching.text: **LLMs can work with many languages and many kinds of input.** The first use of LLMs, in 2017, was **translation** between languages. Translation is now nearly solved for hundreds of languages.
children: A system trained on several languages, such as English, Dutch and Japanese, learns how words go together in general. So it also gets good at very different languages, such as Navajo.
**Multimodal** systems connect different kinds of input, such as text, speech and images. So they can write a caption for a photo or create an image from a spoken description.

teaching.text: **Nobody fully understands what all the weights are doing.** Over about 75 years, people took something that worked a little, changed it so it worked a little better, and kept going. This is like how dogs were bred over a few hundred years into today's breeds. Researchers around the world are now trying to figure out what the weights do. Part of the reason is to build much smaller, less wasteful systems.

**An agentic system is a team of LLMs that talk to each other in English.** An outline LLM plans the answer, and a writing LLM writes it. A critic LLM checks whether each statement follows from the one before it, and a revision LLM goes back and forth with the critic. Sometimes a **controller** agent passes the work from one LLM to the next.
children: The agents also **know computer languages**, such as Python and database languages, because they were trained to predict whole programs too.
Once each LLM is trained, its weights usually **stop changing** while the agents work together. Some new systems are starting to learn their own connections.

Agents share a **common memory**, where they can write and read information. This shared memory gives them a lot of their power. It is also dangerous, because it lets them coordinate in ways nobody planned.

The same tools can also do good work. One agentic system acts as a patient teacher for a Native American language that is nearly lost, even though there is far too little text in that language to train an ordinary LLM.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers

teaching.text: **Predicting the next word is so hard that an LLM needs many layers, and each layer needs many heads working side by side.** A **head** is one expert. In each layer, the knowledge from all the heads is combined to make **improved vectors**. Then the next layer does the same thing again.
children: This is a question for the exam, so the structure matters. **Layers go one after another, from the input to the output. Heads sit side by side inside each layer.**

teaching.text: **A classroom comparison explains heads and layers.** Imagine trying to improve yourself by visiting a series of classes, one class after another.
children: In the first class, every student gives you their own opinion on how to improve. Each student is like a **head**, an expert with its own view.
You then **combine** all of those opinions into one improved version of yourself. Combining the heads' opinions is what a layer does.
Then you go to the next class and do the same thing again. **The classes are the layers.**
In plain terms, layers give an LLM its depth, which is one round of improvement after another. Heads give it width, which is many experts asked at the same time within each round.

teaching.text: **Each head is a set of weights**, and an expert's knowledge is in its weights. Every head in every layer learns how to improve the vectors, so that at the very end the next word can be predicted.
children: Large systems have **a hundred or more layers** and about **a hundred heads** in each layer. That shows how complicated language, vision and the other tasks really are.

The heads and layers are trained the same way as everything else. A sentence like "the dog that ... barks" is taken from text, and the system predicts the next word. If it predicts the wrong word, **every head in every layer** adjusts its weights through backpropagation, so the next prediction is closer to barks.
Training at this size uses enormous resources. In some states, a large share of the water goes to the data centers that run this training.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a rule that is fed its own output again and again.** Numbers go in, the rule acts on them, and numbers come out. Then the output is fed back in as the next input, over and over. The goal is to understand this general structure, not to memorize formulas.
children: In the **harmonic oscillator**, the two numbers are the position x and the velocity v. If x starts at one and v starts at zero, the first step leaves x the same and makes v go down.
x and v **take turns**. First the new x is calculated from the old v. Then the new v is calculated from that new x. Step by step, the rule draws a **cosine** curve for x.

Very different fields, such as finance, use the same idea with different rules. Stock prices are modeled with equations that feed back on themselves, although the real market never follows them exactly.

teaching.text: **Jordan's network combined neural networks with dynamical systems.** Speech production changes over time, so Jordan designed a network whose **output is copied back into its state units**. The state units also keep a fading copy of their own past values.
children: **Plan units** and **state units** feed the hidden layer. The hidden layer feeds the output, and the output loops back into the state units. The same weights are used at every step.
After more than **thirty years of small improvements**, this idea became the **LLM**.

teaching.text: **In an LLM, each layer is the rule.** Each layer applies its weights to every vector, and the next layer works on the result. So **going up through the layers plays the role of time**. If you follow one number up through the layers, it traces a curve, much like the oscillator's curve, though not an exact cosine.
children: So an LLM is like a recurrent network that has been laid out layer by layer. This is just like how the spring's motion was laid out step by step when it was calculated on a computer.
The rule in each layer is the weights of its heads. Those weights are learned through backpropagation by predicting the next word.
Agentic systems also contain loops, such as the loop between the critic and the revision LLM. So dynamical systems show up at every level of AI.
The math of inner products that LLMs depend on was first studied deeply in **quantum mechanics**, about a hundred years ago. So physics and AI are closely connected in more than one way.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: An LLM is given **15 vectors** and asked to predict the **16th**. The vectors can come from anywhere, because the machine only ever sees lists of numbers.
children: They can be **15 words** of a sentence, such as "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," with the next word missing.
They can be **15 frames of a spectrogram**, with the next slice of speech missing.
They can be **15 patches of an image**, read row by row, with the bottom-right patch missing.
They can be **15 amino acids** in a protein. In the B chain of insulin, the amino acid that comes after the first fifteen is the one written Y.

teaching.text: **The same design and the same prediction game work for language, speech, images and proteins.** Whatever the vectors stand for, the job is always to predict what comes next in the sequence.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: English has about 30,000 words, so training an LLM on words takes enormous amounts of data, money and energy. But speakers also know a much smaller system, which is the rules for how vowels and consonants can follow each other to make words. That system uses **only a few dozen sounds**, so an LLM for it can be small enough to study closely.
**A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, sit, shave, cup, dog and fish. The pattern is about sounds, so the silent e in shave does not count.
children: English also allows **clusters**, as in split, flat, black, glad, desk, help and milk. Only certain clusters are allowed, so **sblit**, **lfat**, **desb** and **lapm** are impossible. A product named "desb" would sound un-English right away.
Long words are chains of syllables. **Atlantic** is fine, because t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break. But **tlantic** is impossible, because tl cannot start an English syllable.

teaching.text: **Every language has its own rules for which sounds can follow which**, and speakers pick them up without being taught.
children: **Mandarin** allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, so words like mat, sit and shave are impossible in Mandarin. **Cantonese** also allows a final p, as in cup.
**Russian and Polish** allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, which English never allows.
**Spanish** does not allow a word to start with s and t together. So Spanish speakers add an e to the start of a word like stadium, which keeps each syllable simple.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: Guessing the next letter of an English word shows directly what speakers know about sounds. **After a vowel, almost any letter can come next.** But **at the start of a word, the choices narrow sharply**.
children: After **sp**, only l, r or a vowel can come. After **skr**, or after an **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
After **k**, a vowel or n can come, as in knee. After **sh**, a vowel or r can come, as in shrimp.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the 16th vector.** A GPT that only plays this game learns English sounds and spelling. After a vowel, its predicted probability distribution is **flat**. After skr, the distribution is **sharply peaked**, because English allows almost nothing else there.
children: In plain terms, the knowledge is in the shape of the distribution. It is spread out where English allows many choices, and piled up where English allows only a few.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: You can build an LLM that learns English syllables by **describing it in plain English** to an agentic system, instead of programming it by hand. The request asked for **five layers**, **four heads in each layer**, and **input vectors that are 64 numbers long**.
children: It asked the system to pick **1000 English words at random** and train the LLM on them. Training meant taking each letter, trying to **predict the next letter**, and then improving the weights to predict better.
It also asked the system to show **ten generated words after each step of training**, to reveal what the LLM knew about English at that point.

teaching.text: The agentic system translated the request into its own technical terms. It built a small **character-level transformer**, which is another name for an LLM that works one letter at a time, with **attention heads**.
children: **Attention** means a head looks over the rest of the sequence to decide which items before it matter. This is the same way predicting barks requires paying attention to dog.
The system chose to train on **pronunciations** instead of spellings, so the silent e in shave would not confuse it. It also wrote the program in Python on its own.

teaching.text: The results show how hard the problem is. After training on 1000 words, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, with maybe a few vowels starting to show up in the right places. The suggested next step was to train on **10,000 words** for many more steps.
children: Deciding which sounds can follow which seems easy for any speaker, but it is not easy even for an LLM.

teaching.text: This way of working has a name.
children: **Software 1.0** is writing programs in a programming language such as Python or C.
**Software 2.0** is giving a neural network input data and output data, so the program becomes the network's **weights**, which predict the outputs from the inputs.

**Software 3.0** is using an agentic system, which is a set of LLMs talking to each other and to the user, to build and run a program. Doing this with plain English instructions is called **vibe coding**. It means someone with a good idea no longer needs to hire a programmer to build it.

teaching.text: The first attempt at this kind of problem was **Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication."** Shannon worked by hand and produced sequences of letters that got closer and closer to English. They went from random strings of consonants, to strings with vowels, to strings with real short words.
children: That paper started **information theory**, one of the most important fields in engineering. Information theory is still important for LLMs today.
**Viterbi**, one of the people who developed dynamic programming, published his most famous work in an information theory journal. So the ideas behind backpropagation and LLMs share the same roots.
